selectedComments.author: mcwitt-agent
selectedComments.body:
🤖 Follow-up to #9481: I stopped a push from 81% toward 90% single-rank overlap. Single-rank overlap swings by several points depending on the rank, because GPUs in the rack run at different speeds, and scheduling changes did not beat 81% on rank 0.

The PR tip with its PGLE profile, on one GB200 rack restored from `step-144000`, measures 81.0% overlap on rank 0 ([overlap80-v2-pgle-144k](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/overlap80-v2-pgle-144k)) and 72.5% on rank 37 ([overlap90-v2-rank37-144k](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/overlap90-v2-rank37-144k)). Rank 37 spends 11.55 s per step in compute and rank 0 spends 12.18 s. Rank 37 is 4-6% faster in every kernel family, including the shared-expert MLP and the attention projections, which do identical work on every rank. A faster rank spends the difference waiting inside collectives: on rank 0, the layer-end all-reduce of the RMSNorm weight gradients carries 61 KB and takes 2-7 ms per layer. The two ranks were traced in separate runs, which may have landed on different racks.

Removing a synchronizing collective moves the wait to the next one. I summed the norm-weight gradients once after the layer scan, using one weight copy per batch shard, and counted capacity drops without the per-layer psum. The wait then appeared in the next backward ragged transport. Together with saving the ragged group-size all-gather through the layer remat and re-gathering prefetched MLP weights in a custom_vjp backward, overlap fell to 70.5% and the step grew from 13.72 s to 14.0 s ([overlap90-h-pgle-144k](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/overlap90-h-pgle-144k)). Under its PGLE schedule, that program's loss drifted upward by about 1e-3 by step 144021. The same program without PGLE matched the baseline within 1e-4, so that schedule may expose a race. These changes will not land.

Other negative results, each measured with a PGLE profile built for its own program: XLA's pipelined all-reduce gave 75.2%, re-gathering the MLP weights in the backward instead of prefetching them gave 77.4%, `--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor=90` gave 81.3% (no change), and rebuilding the PR tip's profile from a PGLE-scheduled trace gave 75.8%.

Current belief: #9481, at 81% on rank 0 and a 13.72 s step against the 13.94 s baseline, is the practical limit of scheduling for this model on one rack. A higher target needs a different metric, such as overlap on the slowest rank or overlap excluding peer-wait time. Measuring either requires tracing several ranks in one run, which needs per-process profile file names; the pods run four processes each and share a hostname.

selectedComments.author: ClassicLarry
selectedComments.body:
🤖 **Batch 102: stacking this round's small consistent gains, and the root cause of the single-process stalls**

**Stack4 = candidate 8 + router Adam LR ×0.5 + MuonH gate init ×2 + sqrt-softplus combine + drop-aware combine renorm** (d512, equal steps)

| run | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | median step |
|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 8 | 0 | 0 | 183.5 / 184.5 ms |
| **stack4** | **−0.0042 / −0.0070** | **−0.0056** | 185.0 / 186.6 ms (+1.0%) |

The pieces on their own (2 seeds each; each consistent in sign but under the 0.005 bar):
- router LR ×0.5: −0.0024. The bracket was ×0.1 +0.0030, ×0.25 −0.0011, ×0.5 −0.0024, ×1 0, ×2 +0.0089.
- gate init ×2: −0.0022. The bracket was ×0.5 +0.0013, ×1 0, ×2 −0.0022, ×4 +0.0002.
- sqrt-softplus combine: −0.0021.
- drop renorm: −0.0014. It recovers ≈ 40% of the −0.0035 dropless gain for free.

They add up roughly linearly (sum −0.0081 vs −0.0056 stacked). At fixed time the +1.0% median step costs ≈ 0.0017, so the net is ≈ −0.004. **It clears the 0.005 bar at equal steps, and d768 validation is running** (`lc1-b102-d768-stack4` / `-s1`, vs the d768 candidate 8 reference below).

**d768 candidate 8** (batch 95, widths scaled to hidden, 7325 steps): **2.7197 / 2.7156** (mean 2.7177), **k ≈ 2.2× vs clean KMA** (candidate 7 was 1.82×). First-half latent selection at d768: 2.7199 / 2.7138 (−0.0008), neutral again. That's consistent with d512, so projection vs selection is settled at two scales.

**Closed in this round** (2 seeds each unless noted):

| idea | mean Δ |
|---|---|
| FoX forget gate (bias 4; bias 0 NaNs) | +0.0008; the gate learns f ≈ 0.999 (turns forgetting off), and it is 43% slower from head-dim padding |
| Magma (with MuonH LR ×3 to offset its ≈0.3× average step) | +0.0097 (uncompensated: +0.098) |
| MuonSphere, MuonH LR ×1 / ×0.5 / ×0.25 | +0.027 / +0.013 / +0.060 |
| momentum warmup, cautious WD, slower early upper-layer q/k LR (25% / 4% of training) | +0.0012, +0.0007, 0.0000 / −0.0010 |
| expert init ×0.5 / ×2 | +0.0028 / +0.0015 |
| unigram lm_head bias | +0.0025 |
| token-conditioned router bias; router soft-cap 5 / 10; AttnRes logit soft-cap 5 / 10 | +0.0004; +0.0016 / +0.0002; −0.0012 / −0.0007 |

**Single-process stalls: the root cause is the data loader, not logging or CPU throttling.**
- Throttling: the stall sampler now logs the cgroup's `nr_throttled`, and it is 0 in every stall.
- Summed over all stalls, the busy background threads are the loader's prefetch threads (`_fill_queue_with_batches`): `batched_device_put` (≈ 5.3k samples), `np.stack` (≈ 600) and `backend_compile_and_load` (≈ 390, the loader compiling mid-run). Meanwhile the main thread sits in device↔host copies, and the sampler thread itself gets ≈ 1 sample per 0.5 s. The whole process is starved of the interpreter lock.
- Why: levanter's `CausalLmDataset` / `PrebuiltLmDataset` build **every example with its own `eqx.filter_jit` call** on the CPU backend (128 dispatches per batch, recompiling on new shapes), and prefetch 512 batches ahead in bursts. With 8 processes each builds 1/8 of the batch under its own interpreter lock. With one process driving 8 GPUs, all of it contends with the step dispatch.
- Stalls grow from ≈ 0.4 s early in the run to 3–5 s late.
- **Proposed fix** (not done yet): a batch-level NumPy path in those datasets. It would build a whole batch of examples on host in one vectorized pass instead of 128 jitted calls, with a smaller prefetch buffer. This is a shared-pipeline change, so it would sit behind an explicit option and be checked bit-exact against the current path. With it, ragged's gap should shrink to its own +3% of GPU time (layout pad/zero-fill kernels plus the fused expert kernel at ≈ 1.5× cuBLAS). That would make the −0.0035 dropless gain roughly break-even, and a net win once those kernels are fixed.

[datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
sources.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores: one
Zephyr task per normalized shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the text through the
tokenize stage's own core and matching the Harrier embedding on `id`. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a rerun of the score stage lands at the step's own identity. The
content-type leaves written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `QualityPin` carries
separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file, checked by the
worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed dataset without
moving or rescoring the raw scores. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage run from text against the
same embeddings matched the pinned scores to a maximum difference of 1.6e-3 (mean
2.3e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a 4,096-document batch against the
earlier 32,768.

sources.body:
Allow Iris Kubernetes jobs to request one named NVLink rack through a required job constraint: `nvlink.domain == <rack label>`. Iris keeps the label's case through controller storage. A constrained Pod gets both a node selector and required node affinity for that rack. Kueue can replace the selector while admitting a gang; the affinity keeps the rack requirement. The Pod cannot run on another rack if the requested rack is missing or full.

The focused Iris tests (188) and lint/type checks pass. The local affected-test command (`uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py`) had 4,565 passes and 11 failures; the same 11 failed on clean main on this host. No live placement of this change has been tested.

sources.title: [iris] Route Evalchemy locally and reuse proxy connections
sources.body:
On the serving Iris cluster, Evalchemy resolves each vLLM endpoint through Iris's endpoint API before an evaluation and sends requests to its in-cluster address, bypassing the public capability proxy. Harbor's external Daytona sandboxes keep capability URLs for candidate and hosted judge endpoints. The orchestrator scrapes vLLM metrics directly. The Rust proxy retains up to 256 idle upstream connections per host and closes them after 90 seconds idle.

During five minutes of September 26 eval load, Finelog recorded 7,734 additional hub proxy 502s and 10,749 additional CoreWeave peer proxy 502s. An affected JSON response said `upstream transport error: client error (Connect)`, identifying the Rust proxy's upstream request path. Its upstream pool retained zero idle connections, forcing a new connection after every completed request. Connection churn is a plausible contributor; the historical response does not expose the socket error. In a later run, a serving task was preempted at 20:20:29 UTC. The proxy returned `No endpoint` 404s after its 10-minute registration lease expired and until a replacement registered at 20:35:07. No ready endpoint was registered during that interval. [Incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/529).

[PR #9484](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9484) preserves Evalchemy transport failures in records and gates low-coverage runs. The Rust proxy change requires an updated Iris controller image on the hub and `cw-rno2a` peer.

sources.title: [grug] Hide the ragged MoE transports under compute
sources.body:
Raise the hero step's communication/compute overlap from 60% to 81% of collective time on one rack. The ragged backend now pipelines its two expert chunks, and the model keeps small collectives out of the transports' windows. A profile-guided latency estimate lets XLA place each transport under enough compute.

The hero runs with collective overlap limited to 1, so a single collective can be in flight. Before this change, the ragged transport serialized its chunks behind a barrier, so the first dispatch and first return had no GEMM to hide under. Small collectives also took the only slot inside the MoE section: the transpose rule's two offset all-to-alls, the FSDP gathers of the latent and shared-expert weights, and the router's QB pmin/pmax/histogram reductions. XLA also rematerialized the attention weight gathers after scheduling as exposed synchronous all-gathers. Each commit removes one of these causes:

- The chunks run as a two-stage pipeline, so chunk 1's dispatch overlaps chunk 0's expert MLP and chunk 0's return overlaps chunk 1's.
- The backward takes its transfer offsets from the mirror parameters instead of exchanging them. A test checks that the two parameter sets are each other's transpose.
- The attention projections re-gather their weights for the backward at the JAX level, as ordinary async all-gathers.
- The MLP-section weights are gathered before routing, and the QB statistics run after the routed MLP. A forward-only barrier enforces both, so the gradient reduce-scatters still fuse.

The code changes alone leave overlap near 60% and slow the step by 1.3%. XLA's default estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so it hides a 3-5 ms ragged transport under one GEMM. The last commit adds `pgle_profile.py`, which turns one XProf trace into a latency profile for `--xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`. The README documents the trace, build, and rerun workflow. The profile matches instructions by name, so it is rebuilt for each program and is not committed.

Measured on one GB200 rack restored from the hero's `step-144000`, batch 1024, with production XLA flags. Overlap is kernel-classified, as in the [baseline comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5821773936):

| | overlap | exposed collective | step |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main (2026-09-24 baseline) | 60.5% | 1.51 s | 13.94 s |
| this branch | 60.2% | 1.55 s | 14.13 s |
| this branch + its PGLE profile | 81.0% | 0.88 s | 13.72 s |

The last row is W&B run `overlap80-v2-pgle-144k`. Its step time is 1.6% shorter than the baseline's. Loss matches the baseline to within 3e-4 at every step. Collective busy time rises from 3.8 to 4.6 s, because a transport overlapped with a GEMM runs slower. The trace covers only rack-local collectives, and the 11-rack production program would need its own profile. The production recipe still runs without PGLE, so deploying these commits alone would slow the hero rather than speed it up.

Part of #8317

sources.title: [eval] Preserve Evalchemy transport failures in records
sources.body:
Pin Evalchemy to `4a2d6390`, which writes `failure_category` for model transport, agent timeout, and grader infrastructure failures. Marin rebuilds native FineStore samples from Evalchemy's raw artifacts to restore missing prompts; that rebuild previously replaced infrastructure-error markers with empty model outputs. Preserve those markers and recompute metrics from successfully scored items, including the `math500` result alias for the `MATH500` task.

A September 26 math500 run using this Evalchemy revision recorded 288 `model_transport` failures among 500 source samples. Marin's rebuilt archive stored those rows as empty outputs, and its record reported `errors={}` and 500/500 scored. For any task with an infrastructure error, fewer than 90% scored items among its intended attempted items now makes the run `infra_failed`, even if other errors also contributed to the missing scores. The record retains metrics and coverage, and pipeline steps do not cache the run as successful. Runs meeting the threshold keep their scored results.

[PR #9480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9480) changes Iris routing and proxy connection reuse to reduce transport failures. This PR preserves and reports failures that still occur. [Incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/529).
